claim: Protein half-lives were determined for over 5100 proteins in rat primary hippocampal cultures ranging from <1 to >20 days.
source: We used dynamic SILAC to determine half-lives of over 5100 proteins in rat primary hippocampal cultures as well as in neuron-enriched and glia-enriched cultures ranging from <1 to >20 days.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of proteins analyzed and the range of half-lives measured.

claim: Membrane proteins were relatively shorter-lived compared to the population.
source: In contrast to synaptic proteins, membrane proteins were relatively shorter-lived and mitochondrial proteins were longer-lived compared to the population.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding from the experimental data.

claim: Mitochondrial proteins were longer-lived compared to the population.
source: In contrast to synaptic proteins, membrane proteins were relatively shorter-lived and mitochondrial proteins were longer-lived compared to the population.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding from the experimental data.

claim: Half-lives correlate with protein functions.
source: Half-lives also correlate with protein functions and the dynamics of the complexes they are incorporated in.
evidence: The abstract states this correlation based on the study's findings.

claim: Half-lives correlate with the dynamics of the complexes proteins are incorporated in.
source: Half-lives also correlate with protein functions and the dynamics of the complexes they are incorporated in.
evidence: The abstract states this correlation based on the study's findings.

claim: Proteins in glia possessed shorter half-lives than the same proteins in neurons.
source: Proteins in glia possessed shorter half-lives than the same proteins in neurons.
evidence: The abstract directly states this comparative finding.

claim: The presence of glia sped up or slowed down the turnover of neuronal proteins.
source: The presence of glia sped up or slowed down the turnover of neuronal proteins.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding about environmental effects.

claim: Both the cell-type of origin and the nature of the extracellular environment have potent influences on protein turnover.
source: Our results demonstrate that both the cell-type of origin as well as the nature of the extracellular environment have potent influences on protein turnover.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this statement based on the study's findings.

claim: Protein turnover allows for the removal of damaged proteins and their replacement by new proteins.
source: Protein turnover allows for the removal of damaged proteins and their replacement by new proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Continuous protein turnover is required to enable cells to dynamically adjust their proteome according to internal and external perturbations and signals.
source: In addition, continuous protein turnover is required and exploited to enable cells to dynamically adjust their proteome according to internal and external perturbations and signals.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Proteome remodeling using protein synthesis and degradation is required for learning and memory formation in the brain.
source: In the brain, proteome remodeling using protein synthesis and degradation is required for learning and memory formation (Sutton and Schuman, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Several forms of synaptic plasticity studied in vitro require protein synthesis and protein degradation.
source: In addition, several forms of synaptic plasticity studied in vitro also require protein synthesis and protein degradation (Ehlers, 2003; Kang and Schuman, 1996; Rosenberg et al., 2014; Schanzenbächer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Price et al. (2010) measured turnover rates for 1010 proteins with an average half-life of ~9 days in the mouse brain using in vivo metabolic 15N-labelling.
source: Price et al. (2010) used in vivo metabolic 15N-labelling and the subsequent mass spectrometric analysis of whole brain homogenates to derive the turnover rates for 1010 proteins (average half-life =~9 days) in the mouse brain.
evidence: This describes findings from a cited previous study.

claim: Cohen et al. (2013) measured relatively shorter half-lives for 2802 brain proteins with an average half-life of ~5 days using in vitro metabolic labeling of primary cortical cultures.
source: Another study used in vitro metabolic labeling of primary cortical cultures to measure relatively shorter half-lives for 2802 brain proteins (average half-life =~5 days; (Cohen et al., 2013)).
evidence: This describes findings from a cited previous study.

claim: Proteins can show very different turnover rates in different tissues.
source: It is known that proteins can show very different turnover rates in different tissues (Price et al., 2010) or different cell types (Mathieson et al., 2018) of the same organism, but little is known about protein turnover rates in different cell types of the brain.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Proteins can show very different turnover rates in different cell types of the same organism.
source: It is known that proteins can show very different turnover rates in different tissues (Price et al., 2010) or different cell types (Mathieson et al., 2018) of the same organism, but little is known about protein turnover rates in different cell types of the brain.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Little is known about protein turnover rates in different cell types of the brain.
source: It is known that proteins can show very different turnover rates in different tissues (Price et al., 2010) or different cell types (Mathieson et al., 2018) of the same organism, but little is known about protein turnover rates in different cell types of the brain.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: The median half-life of proteins in mixed cultures was 5.4 days.
source: The proteins we analyzed exhibited a range of half-lives from <1 day to >20 days; the median half-life was 5.4 days.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the study's data.

claim: The distribution of protein half-lives is right skewed, reflecting a long-tail of proteins with longer than average half-lives.
source: The distribution of protein half-lives, shown in Figure 1B, is right skewed, reflecting a long-tail of proteins with longer than average half-lives.
evidence: This describes the distribution pattern observed in the data and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Across the complete set of protein half-lives in mixed cultures, a mean SE of the rate constant of ~0.007 and a median R2 of 0.96 were obtained.
source: Across the complete set of protein half-lives in mixed cultures, we obtained a mean SE of the rate constant of ~0.007 and a median R2 of 0.96 demonstrating an accurate determination of protein half-lives.
evidence: These are statistical measures from the study's data analysis.

claim: The half-lives obtained with FUNCAT-PLA were well-correlated with the half-lives obtained with MS (Pearson correlation = 0.983).
source: For all four proteins examined, the half-lives obtained by the FUNCAT-PLA analysis were well-correlated with the half-lives obtained with MS (Pearson correlation = 0.983; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct comparison of two measurement methods with a correlation coefficient.

claim: The half-lives obtained with FUNCAT-PLA were systematically shorter than those obtained with MS.
source: We noted, however, that the half-lives obtained with FUNCAT-PLA were systematically shorter.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the two measurement methods.

claim: The systematically shorter half-lives obtained with FUNCAT-PLA could be owing to a reduced stability of the AHA-containing proteins or the azide group used for tagging or other factors.
source: This could be owing to a reduced stability of the AHA-containing proteins or the azide group used for tagging or other factors, as discussed below.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of the observed difference.

claim: Proteins associated with the nucleus exhibited a shorter than average half-life.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, many groups exhibited a wide range of protein half-lives that were not significantly different from the population average. An exception to this were proteins associated with the nucleus as well as several groups of membrane proteins, including those associated with the plasma membrane, the Golgi apparatus membrane and the ER membrane which all exhibited a shorter than average half-life.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Proteins associated with the plasma membrane exhibited a shorter than average half-life.
source: An exception to this were proteins associated with the nucleus as well as several groups of membrane proteins, including those associated with the plasma membrane, the Golgi apparatus membrane and the ER membrane which all exhibited a shorter than average half-life.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Proteins associated with the Golgi apparatus membrane exhibited a shorter than average half-life.
source: An exception to this were proteins associated with the nucleus as well as several groups of membrane proteins, including those associated with the plasma membrane, the Golgi apparatus membrane and the ER membrane which all exhibited a shorter than average half-life.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Proteins associated with the ER membrane exhibited a shorter than average half-life.
source: An exception to this were proteins associated with the nucleus as well as several groups of membrane proteins, including those associated with the plasma membrane, the Golgi apparatus membrane and the ER membrane which all exhibited a shorter than average half-life.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Mitochondrial proteins exhibited significantly longer half-lives than all other groups.
source: Mitochondrial proteins also deviated from the population average: they exhibited significantly longer half-lives than all other groups.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The observation that mitochondrial proteins have longer half-lives is counter-intuitive given the exposure of mitochondrial proteins to elevated levels of reactive oxygen species.
source: This was a counter-intuitive observation given the exposure of mitochondrial proteins to elevated levels of reactive oxygen species (Adam-Vizi and Chinopoulos, 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding in light of existing knowledge.

claim: Synaptic proteins as a group do not exhibit significantly different half-lives from the population.
source: Lastly, despite their remote location within axonal and dendritic arbors, we found that synaptic proteins as a group do not exhibit significantly different half-lives from the population (Figure 4—source data 1; see below and Figure 4 for more discussion of individual synaptic protein half-lives).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Receptors, signaling molecules, cell adhesion molecules, and proteins involved in stimulus response and cell communication were over-represented in the segment of comparably short-lived (<3 days) proteins.
source: For example, receptors, signaling molecules, cell adhesion molecules, and proteins involved in stimulus response and cell communication were over-represented in the segment of comparably short-lived (<3 days) proteins.
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology analysis of the data.

claim: Ribosomal proteins were enriched in a group with relatively long half-lives (6–11 days).
source: Ribosomal proteins were enriched in a group with relatively long half-lives (6–11 days).
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology analysis of the data.

claim: Proteins involved in energy metabolism were over-represented amongst the most long-lived (12–15 days) groups.
source: Amongst the most long-lived (12–15 days) groups we found a significant over-representation of proteins involved in energy metabolism.
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology analysis of the data.

claim: Histones were over-represented in the long-lived group, consistent with previous reports.
source: In this long-lived group there was also an over-representation of histones and nuclear pore proteins, consistent with previous reports (Savas et al., 2012; Toyama et al., 2013).
evidence: This finding is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: Nuclear pore proteins were over-represented in the long-lived group, consistent with previous reports.
source: In this long-lived group there was also an over-representation of histones and nuclear pore proteins, consistent with previous reports (Savas et al., 2012; Toyama et al., 2013).
evidence: This finding is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: Receptors for the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate (GluR1, GluR2, GluR3, GluR6, NMDAR1, NMDAR1B, mGluR3, mGluR5, and mGlusR7) exhibit shorter half-lives than the global protein population average.
source: We note that the receptors for the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate (GluR1, GluR2, GluR3, GluR6, NMDAR1, NMDAR1B, mGluR3, mGluR5, and mGlusR7) exhibit shorter half-lives than the global protein population average (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Receptors for the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA exhibited half-lives similar to the population average.
source: while receptors for the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA exhibited half-lives similar to the population average (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Relatively short half-lives were observed for most of the cell adhesion molecules identified, including most neuroligins (NLGN) and neurexins (NRXN) as well as N-cadherin.
source: Relatively short half-lives were also observed for most of the cell adhesion molecules we identified, including most neuroligins (NLGN) and neurexins (NRXN) as well as N-cadherin.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: More long-lived proteins were found in the pre-synaptic compartment.
source: More long-lived proteins were found in the pre-synaptic compartment.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Amongst the most long-lived synaptic molecules are those associated with synaptic vesicles and vesicle processing including the synapsins, the synaptic vesicle transporter family Sv2 as well as the Munc proteins.
source: Amongst the most long-lived synaptic molecules are those associated with synaptic vesicles and vesicle processing including the synapsins, the synaptic vesicle transporter family Sv2 as well as the Munc proteins (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Individual protein isoforms and members within a protein family can exhibit very different half-lives.
source: We also noted in some cases that individual protein isoforms as well as members within a protein family could exhibit very different half-lives, e.g. the synaptotagmins (Syt), the syntaxins (STX) and even CamK2 subunits (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: On average, proteins that are co-members of a complex have more similar half-lives than randomly selected proteins.
source: We examined 314 protein complexes (composed of >5 proteins) and found that on average, proteins that are co-members of a complex have more similar half-lives than randomly selected proteins (Figure 5A; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The variability of protein half-lives within complexes does not correlate with the number of constituents in a complex.
source: We found that the variability of protein half-lives within complexes does not correlate with the number of constituents in a complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The spliceosome constituents exhibited the fastest turnover of the four complexes examined (spliceosome, ribosome, nuclear pore complex, ATP synthase).
source: At the dynamic extreme is the spliceosome; here were observed that the spliceosome constituents exhibited the fastest turnover of the four complexes examined.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis of specific protein complexes.

claim: For the ATP synthase, the longest average half-life was observed among the four complexes examined.
source: At the static extreme, we placed the ATP synthase and the small and the large subunit of the ribosome. Notably, for the ATP synthase, we observed the longest average half-life.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis of specific protein complexes.

claim: The highest variation of subunit half-lives was found in the nuclear pore complex.
source: The NPC is located in the center of the dynamism axis, as it contains both a static core as wells as dynamic outer filaments. Correspondingly, we found the highest variation of subunit half-lives in the NPC.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis of specific protein complexes.

claim: Both the dynamic spliceosome and the static ribosome sub-complexes displayed similar subunit half-life variations.
source: However, both the dynamic spliceosome and the static ribosome sub-complexes displayed similar subunit half-life variations.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis of specific protein complexes.

claim: Protein degradation and protein stability have been linked to intrinsic sequence properties, such as the N-terminal amino acid, denoted as 'N-end rule'.
source: Indeed, protein degradation and protein stability have been linked to intrinsic sequence properties, such as the N-terminal amino acid, denoted as 'N-end rule' (Bachmair et al., 1986; Gibbs et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Sequence analysis revealed no significantly over- or under-represented N-terminal amino acids in the fraction of short-lived proteins or long-lived proteins.
source: Sequence analysis revealed no significantly over- or under-represented N-terminal amino acids in the fraction of short-lived proteins (10% of proteins with shortest half-lives) or long-lived proteins (10% of proteins with longest half-lives), respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the N-terminal sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: More proteins with a destabilizing N-terminal amino acid were found in the fraction of long-lived proteins compared to short-lived proteins.
source: Interestingly, we found more proteins with a destabilizing N-terminal amino acid in the fraction of long-lived proteins compared to short-lived proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the N-terminal sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In primary hippocampal cultures, N-terminal sequence properties seem to have little impact on protein lifetimes when compared to protein functions and localization.
source: In primary hippocampal cultures, N-terminal sequence properties seem to have little impact on protein lifetimes when compared to protein functions and localization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the N-terminal sequence analysis results.

claim: The proteomes of neuron-enriched and glia-enriched cultures were clearly different from the mixed cultures.
source: The proteomes of these neuron-enriched and glia-enriched cultures were clearly different from the mixed cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,H)
evidence: This is a finding from the proteomic analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,H.

claim: The glia-enriched cultures are strongly enriched in astrocytes and microglia, while markers for oligodendrocytes do not show a consistent enrichment.
source: Proteomic analysis further revealed that the glia-enriched cultures are strongly enriched in astrocytes and microglia, while markers for oligodendrocytes do not show a consistent enrichment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E; see also Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the proteomic analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: At the population level, the proteins extracted from the glial-enriched cultures exhibited a significantly faster turnover than the proteins extracted from either the neuron-enriched or mixed cultures.
source: We found that, at the population level, the proteins extracted from the glial-enriched cultures exhibited a significantly faster turnover than the proteins extracted from either the neuron-enriched or mixed cultures, which were much more similar to one another (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was a 75% overlap in proteomes between the glial-enriched proteome and neuron-enriched proteome.
source: This global difference in turnover between the proteins from the glial-enriched samples and the other two samples cannot be explained by simple differences in their respective proteomes, as there was an 75% and 78% overlap in proteomes between the glial-enriched proteome and neuron-enriched and mixed proteomes, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the proteomic comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was a 78% overlap in proteomes between the glial-enriched proteome and mixed proteome.
source: This global difference in turnover between the proteins from the glial-enriched samples and the other two samples cannot be explained by simple differences in their respective proteomes, as there was an 75% and 78% overlap in proteomes between the glial-enriched proteome and neuron-enriched and mixed proteomes, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the proteomic comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A comparison of the turnover rates in glial-enriched cultures vs mixed cultures revealed a systematic shift of almost the entire proteome to faster half-lives in glial-enriched cultures.
source: A comparison of the turnover rates in glial-enriched cultures vs mixed cultures revealed a systematic shift of almost the entire proteome to faster half-lives in glial-enriched cultures (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There is no significant cell division of glia in the confluent mature cultures.
source: We considered whether the faster turnover observed in glial-enriched cultures could be related to ongoing cell-division of glia cells, but, as noted above, there is no significant cell division of glia in the confluent mature cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: The heavy isotopically labelled form of Histone H3.1 is only produced by cell division and not by protein turnover in post-mitotic cells.
source: We further explored the issue of cell division by examining the half-life of Histone H3.1 in the mixed vs. glia-enriched cultures. The heavy isotopically labelled form of Histone H3.1 is only produced by cell division and not by protein turnover in post-mitotic cells (Ahmad and Henikoff, 2002; Schwartz and Ahmad, 2005; Wu et al., 1982).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Similar long half-lives for Histone H3.1 were obtained in mixed cultures (11.6 days) and glia-enriched cultures (11.2 days).
source: Similar long half-lives for Histone H3.1 were obtained in mixed cultures (11.6 days) and glia-enriched cultures (11.2 days) demonstrating that a similar low rate of cell division takes place in both culture types and that cell division cannot account for the faster protein turnover in glia cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5B.

claim: 169 proteins exhibited a significantly faster turnover in mixed cultures compared to neuron-enriched cultures.
source: A comparison of the turnover rates of proteins identified in both the neuron-enriched proteome and the mixed-culture proteome revealed 169 proteins that exhibited a significantly faster turnover in mixed cultures as well as 68 proteins that exhibited a significantly faster turnover in neuron-enriched cultures (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: 68 proteins exhibited a significantly faster turnover in neuron-enriched cultures compared to mixed cultures.
source: A comparison of the turnover rates of proteins identified in both the neuron-enriched proteome and the mixed-culture proteome revealed 169 proteins that exhibited a significantly faster turnover in mixed cultures as well as 68 proteins that exhibited a significantly faster turnover in neuron-enriched cultures (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Proteins with faster turnover rates in mixed compared to neuron-enriched cultures were significantly over-represented in functional groups that represent ribosomal proteins, cytoplasmic translation, the extracellular matrix and focal adhesion.
source: We found that proteins with faster turnover rates in mixed compared to neuron-enriched cultures were significantly over-represented in functional groups that represent ribosomal proteins, cytoplasmic translation, the extracellular matrix and focal adhesion (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Proteins with faster turnover rates in neuron-enriched cultures were significantly over-represented in functional groups related to glycolytic processes, the regulation of neurotransmitter levels, axon terminus and myelin sheath.
source: Further, we found that proteins with faster turnover rates in neuron-enriched cultures were significantly over-represented in functional groups related to glycolytic processes, the regulation of neurotransmitter levels, axon terminus and myelin sheath (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: A majority of the enzymes in the glycolysis pathway exhibited faster turnover in neuron-enriched cultures.
source: Within the glycolysis pathway, we discovered that a majority of the enzymes exhibited faster turnover in neuron-enriched cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Astrocytes provide lactate to neurons.
source: It has been demonstrated that astrocytes provide lactate (which can be converted to pyruvate by the lactate dehydrogenase) to neurons (Magistretti and Pellerin, 1999; Mason, 2017)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The relative paucity of glia in the neuron-enriched cultures would lead to the loss of astrocyte-derived lactate and could lead to enhanced metabolic activity of the neuron's own glycolytic axis, and a resulting faster turnover.
source: the relative paucity of glia in the neuron-enriched cultures would lead to the loss of astrocyte-derived lactate and could lead to enhanced metabolic activity of the neuron's own glycolytic axis, and a resulting faster turnover (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is an interpretation/speculation about the mechanism shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Several proteins related to the synaptic vesicle cycle as well as neurotransmitter synthetic enzymes exhibited a faster turnover in neuron-enriched cultures relative to mixed cultures.
source: Within the synapse, we noted that several proteins related to the synaptic vesicle cycle as well as neurotransmitter synthetic enzymes exhibited a faster turnover in neuron-enriched cultures relative to mixed cultures (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The protein turnover rates in neuron-enriched cultures with and without conditioned medium were very similar to one another, with just a few proteins showing altered turnover.
source: When we compared the protein turnover rates in the two conditions, we found that they were very similar to one another, with just a few proteins showing altered turnover as a result of the presence or absence of pre-conditioned medium (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The proteins that had a faster turnover in neuron-enriched cultures compared to mixed cultures did not show different turnover kinetics in neuron-enriched cultures with and without conditioned medium.
source: We also noted that the proteins that had a faster turnover in neuron-enriched cultures compared to mixed cultures (see Figure 6D) did not show different turnover kinetics in neuron-enriched cultures with and without conditioned medium (e.g. glycolytic enzymes and proteins depicted in Figure 6H; see also Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis.

claim: The differences in protein turnover between neuron-enriched and neuron-glia cultures likely arise from physical/mechanical interactions between the cells, presumably owing to adhesive interactions and its associated signaling.
source: These data indicate that the differences in protein turnover we observe between neuron-enriched and neuron-glia cultures likely arise from physical/mechanical interactions between the cells, presumably owing to adhesive interactions and its associated signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the conditioned medium experiment results.

claim: A median half-life of 5.4 days was obtained in mixed cultures in this study.
source: All in all, we obtained half-life measurements for over 5100 protein groups which exhibited a range of half-lives from <1 day to >20 days, with a median half-life of 5.4 days in mixed cultures.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the study's data.

claim: Cohen et al. (2013) obtained a similar half-life distribution (median = 4.2 days) by measuring the turnover of 2802 protein groups from mixed cortical cultures.
source: A similar half-life distribution (median = 4.2 days) was obtained by Cohen et al. (2013) who measured the turnover of 2802 protein groups from mixed cortical cultures.
evidence: This describes findings from a cited previous study for comparison.

claim: Mathieson et al. (2018) reported clearly shorter half-lives for primary mouse embryonic neurons (median = 1.9 days).
source: A recent study by Mathieson et al. (2018) reported clearly shorter half-lives for primary mouse embryonic neurons (median = 1.9 days).
evidence: This describes findings from a cited previous study for comparison.

claim: The shorter half-lives reported by Mathieson et al. (2018) are likely explained by the relative immaturity of the cultures and the relative short time in vitro.
source: These shorter half-lives are likely explained by the relative immaturity of the cultures (prepared from embryonic rather than postnatal neurons) and the relative short time in vitro (5 days vs. 18–19 days).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differences between studies.

claim: A gene-wise comparison between in vitro and in vivo protein half-lives revealed a significant correlation (Spearman rank correlation = 0.62, p<0.001).
source: We further compared the protein half-lives determined by our in vitro study in mixed cultures to half-lives of mouse brain proteins that were previously determined by in vivo metabolic labelling. Though proteins were clearly longer-lived in vivo (average half-life ~9 days) compared to in vitro, a gene-wise comparison revealed a significant correlation between protein half-lives (Spearman rank correlation = 0.62, p<0.001; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The systematic offset between in vivo and in vitro half-lives could be explained by the different experimental approach, species, cellular compositions and environments as well as by the different ages of the investigated cells.
source: The systematic offset could be explained by the different experimental approach, species (mouse versus rat), cellular compositions and environments as well as by the different ages of the investigated cells.
evidence: This is speculation about the causes of the observed differences.

claim: Visscher et al. (2016) reported shorter half-lives for proteins in young cells (C. elegans larvae) compared to older cells (adult C. elegans).
source: Visscher et al. (2016) recently reported shorter half-lives for proteins in young cells (C. elegans larvae) compared to older cells (adult C. elegans).
evidence: This describes findings from a cited previous study.

claim: The ranked half-lives of the proteins determined via MS and FUNCAT-PLA were very well correlated.
source: We found that the ranked half-lives of the proteins determined via MS and FUNCAT-PLA were very well correlated.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation experiment.

claim: Reasons for the offset between MS and FUNCAT-PLA half-lives could include a relative instability of the azide group or AHA-containing proteins, or an increased sensitivity of the AHA-labeling to detect the rapid degradation of misfolded proteins which are missed by the continuous SILAC labelling.
source: Reasons for this offset could include a relative instability of the azide group or AHA-containing proteins, or an increased sensitivity of the AHA-labeling to detect the rapid degradation of misfolded proteins which are missed by the continuous SILAC labelling (also discussed below).
evidence: This is speculation about the causes of the observed differences.

claim: Protein turnover is influenced by the cellular location of the protein.
source: Analysis of our dynamic SILAC data revealed that protein turnover is influenced by the cellular location of the protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the data analysis.

claim: Systematic differences in protein turnover might result from different major degradation mechanisms for cytosolic and membrane proteins as well as the unique quality control mechanism of mitochondria by fission and fusion.
source: These systematic differences in protein turnover might result from different major degradation mechanisms for cytosolic and membrane proteins (Jin et al., 2018; Tai and Schuman, 2008) as well as the unique quality control mechanism of mitochondria by fission and fusion (Cagalinec et al., 2013; Gomes and Scorrano, 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations.

claim: Protein lifetimes evolved in a way that proteins involved in internal and external signal response are short-lived to enable faster and more fine-tuned regulation, while proteins that serve more steady functions in the cell are longer-lived in order to save energy.
source: This finding supports the idea that protein lifetimes evolved evolutionary in a way that proteins involved in internal and external signal response are short-lived to enable faster and more fine-tuned regulation, while proteins that serve more steady functions in the cell are longer-lived in order to save energy that is required for protein synthesis and degradation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional analysis findings.

claim: Cohen et al. (2013) showed that interacting proteins have more similar half-lives compared to non-interacting proteins in primary cortical neurons.
source: Cohen et al. (2013) showed that interacting proteins have more similar half-lives compared to non-interacting proteins in primary cortical neurons.
evidence: This describes findings from a cited previous study.

claim: Protein complexes differ greatly in their biogenesis, assembly and disassembly kinetics, and these differences might be reflected in different mean half-lives between complexes or variability of half-lives within complexes.
source: Protein complexes differ greatly in their biogenesis, assembly and disassembly kinetics, and these differences might be reflected in different mean half-lives between complexes or variability of half-lives within complexes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the relationship between complex dynamics and protein half-lives.

claim: The observed half-lives of nuclear pore complex constituents are in agreement with previous observations of subunit stability.
source: We detected 10 of these proteins and found that the observed half-lives correlate very well with previous observations of subunit stability (Figure 5D,F; Beck and Hurt, 2017).
evidence: This finding is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: The ribosome exhibited substantial variability in the half-lives of its constituents, suggesting the possibility that some ribosomal proteins may be exchanged to repair or even specialize ribosomes in subcellular compartments.
source: Surprisingly, the ribosome, a canonical stable cellular complex where the 40S and 60S subunits are thought to be assembled 'for life' in the nucleus and nucleolus, exhibited substantial variability in the half-lives of its constituents, suggesting the possibility that some ribosomal proteins may be exchanged to repair (Pulk et al., 2010) or even specialize ribosomes (Xue and Barna, 2012) in subcellular compartments (Holt and Schuman, 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with supporting citations.

claim: The half-lives measured do not necessarily represent a single functional state for the proteins.
source: The above results must be interpreted with the caveat that we do not know if the half-lives we measured represent a single functional state for the proteins.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: McShane et al. (2016) demonstrated that ~10% of the proteins show non-exponential decay kinetics with a faster degradation in the first hours after synthesis in mouse fibroblasts.
source: A recent study in mouse fibroblasts demonstrated that ~ 10% of the proteins show non-exponential decay kinetics with a faster degradation in the first hours after synthesis (McShane et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes findings from a cited previous study.

claim: The dynamic SILAC approach used does not allow accurate distinction between different sub-populations of the same protein that have different stabilities.
source: The dynamic SILAC approach we used here does not allow us to accurately distinguish between different sub-populations of the same protein that have different stabilities.
evidence: This is a limitation of the methodology acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Unstable proteins are degraded shortly after synthesis and represent a low abundant sub-population in the whole cell lysate and contribute less to the measured MS signals compared to the corresponding stable protein population.
source: As unstable proteins are degraded shortly after synthesis, they represent a low abundant sub-population in the whole cell lysate and contribute less to the measured MS signals compared to the corresponding stable protein population.
evidence: This is an explanation of a methodological limitation.

claim: Toyama et al. (2013) investigated turnover rates for nuclear proteins in different brain cell types and observed faster protein turnover for glia cells compared to neurons.
source: Others have investigated turnover rates for nuclear proteins in different brain cell types and also observed faster protein turnover for glia cells compared to neurons (Toyama et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes findings from a cited previous study.

claim: Most of the changes in half-life between neuron-enriched and mixed cultures are likely due to adhesive interactions with glial cells, rather than secreted factors.
source: We believe that most of the changes in half-life are likely due to adhesive interactions with glial cells, rather than secreted factors, as there were no big differences in turnover when we compared neuron-enriched cultures treated, or not, with glial conditioned medium.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the conditioned medium experiment results.

claim: In the absence of glia cells, neurons lack lactate supplied from glia and thus require increased glycolytic activity to produce pyruvate.
source: In the absence of glia cells, neurons lack lactate supplied from glia (by the glia-neuron lactate shuttle), and thus require increased glycolytic activity to produce pyruvate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism underlying the observed changes.

claim: The observed increase in turnover of glycolytic enzymes might reflect increased glycolytic activity in neurons lacking glial lactate supply.
source: The observed increase in turnover of glycolytic enzymes might reflect this increased activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: A correlation between turnover and the activity of individual proteins was recently demonstrated in yeast.
source: A similar correlation between turnover and the activity of individual proteins was recently demonstrated in yeast (Martin-Perez and Villén, 2017).
evidence: This describes findings from a cited previous study.

claim: Mature primary neuronal and glial cultures mimic the physiology of cells in-vivo and are an important system to study the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie the physiological and pathophysiological function of neuronal networks.
source: Mature primary neuronal and glial cultures mimic the physiology of cells in-vivo and are an important system to study the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie the physiological and pathophysiological function of neuronal networks.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the experimental system.

claim: Glia cells in the mature cultures do not undergo cell division, owing to the confluence and maturity of the cultures.
source: the latter of which do not undergo cell division, owing to the confluence and maturity of the cultures, see Materials and methods and Figure 6—figure supplement 5
evidence: This is a finding about the culture conditions shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: A small amount of 'light' medium was retained and an excess of 'heavy' medium was added to reduce cellular stress, yielding a final 4:1 ratio of heavy to light amino acids.
source: To reduce cellular stress (see Materials and methods), we retained a small amount of the 'light' medium and an excess of 'heavy' medium was added, yielding a final 4:1 ratio of heavy to light amino acids.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the experimental design.

claim: Following the medium switch, mostly 'heavy' arginine and lysine are incorporated into nascent proteins while the fraction of 'light' proteins decays over time.
source: Note that following the medium switch, mostly 'heavy' arginine and lysine are incorporated into nascent proteins while the fraction of 'light' proteins decays over time.
evidence: This describes the principle of the SILAC labeling approach.

claim: A correction factor was developed for each peptide using the probability of the incorporation of a 'light' amino acid into a nascent protein from peptides containing two arginines or lysines due to a missed tryptic cleavage site.
source: As the medium contained residual 'light' amino acids, we developed a correction factor for each peptide using the probability of the incorporation of a 'light' amino acid into a nascent protein from peptides containing two arginines or lysines due to a missed tryptic cleavage site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes a methodological innovation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: For extremely short-lived proteins, where the data could not be accurately fit by an exponential decay curve, a half-life of <1 day was assigned.
source: For extremely short-lived proteins, where the data could not be accurately fit by an exponential decay curve, we assigned a half–life of <1 day.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision in data analysis.

claim: Previous studies demonstrated that 2 hr AHA incorporation is not toxic to cells and does not affect global protein synthesis or degradation rates.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that 2 hr AHA incorporation is not toxic to cells and does not affect global protein synthesis or degradation rates (Dieterich et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited previous study.

claim: GM130 exhibited a measured half-life of 1.9 days by FUNCAT-PLA.
source: For both GM130 and LaminB1, proteins associated with Golgi and nuclear function, respectively, a decrement in the number of labelled puncta was observed over days, yielding measured half-lives of 1.9 and 4.4 days, respectively (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a measurement from the FUNCAT-PLA validation experiment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: LaminB1 exhibited a measured half-life of 4.4 days by FUNCAT-PLA.
source: For both GM130 and LaminB1, proteins associated with Golgi and nuclear function, respectively, a decrement in the number of labelled puncta was observed over days, yielding measured half-lives of 1.9 and 4.4 days, respectively (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a measurement from the FUNCAT-PLA validation experiment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The spliceosome is a highly dynamic complex that assembles for each splicing event and then disassembles again afterwards.
source: The spliceosome is a highly dynamic complex that assembles for each splicing event and then disassembles again afterwards.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the spliceosome.

claim: The spliceosome proteins exhibit a mean turnover of ~4.7 days, which is faster than the global population of proteins measured.
source: We found that these proteins exhibit a mean turnover of ~4.7 days, which is faster than the global population of proteins we measured.
evidence: This is a finding from the complex analysis.

claim: Ribosomal proteins are synthesized in the cytoplasm and subsequently assembled into the large and small ribosomal subunits in the nucleus and nucleolus.
source: Ribosomal proteins are synthesized in the cytoplasm and subsequently assembled into the large and small ribosomal subunits in the nucleus and nucleolus, where they interact with a variety of ribosomal assembly proteins and ribosomal RNA (Peña et al., 2017), before they are released back into the cytoplasm where they drive protein synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome biogenesis supported by a citation.

claim: The ribosomal subunits themselves are considered to be stable throughout their life-time.
source: Depending on the translational activity, the small and large ribosomal subunits can associate and dissociate, but the subunits themselves are considered to be stable throughout their life-time.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome stability.

claim: The ribosome proteins exhibited a mean half-life of 7.8 days across all subunits.
source: We obtained half-lives for 70 of the 76 ribosomal proteins annotated in the structure, which exhibited a mean half-life of 7.8 days across all subunits (Figure 5C,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the complex analysis shown in Figure 5C,F.

claim: The ATP synthase assembles in a step-wise manner with the membrane-embedded rotor as well as the soluble stalk and head domains produced and assembled independently.
source: The ATP synthase assembles in a step-wise manner. The membrane-embedded rotor as well as the soluble stalk and head domains are produced and assembled independently, and full ATP synthase assembly is a finely-tuned process dependent on the energy demand of the cell (Kucharczyk et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATP synthase assembly supported by a citation.

claim: The ATP synthase protein subunits exhibit a mean half-life of 11.2 days.
source: The protein subunits exhibit a relatively limited range of half-lives with a mean half-live of 11.2 days, with head and stalk subunits displaying more similar half-lives when compared to the whole complex.
evidence: This is a finding from the complex analysis.

claim: The nuclear pore complex is a huge membrane-spanning protein complex that comprises static scaffold regions, intermediate adopter regions as well as highly dynamic regions.
source: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is a huge membrane-spanning protein complex that comprises static scaffold regions, intermediate adopter regions as well as highly dynamic regions (Rabut et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NPC supported by a citation.

claim: Nup62 displayed the shortest half-life of the observed NPC subunits.
source: In contrast, the protein Nup62 displayed the shortest half-life of the observed NPC subunits.
evidence: This is a finding from the complex analysis.

claim: Nup62, as part of the Nup54/58/62 channel trimer at the center of the core, is known to dissociate easily from the complex.
source: Nup62, as part of the Nup54/58/62 channel trimer at the center of the core, is known to dissociate easily from the complex (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Sec13 is a component of the NPC and also a stoichiometric member of the COPII coat.
source: However, Sec13 is also a stoichiometric member of the COPII coat so we cannot attribute the observed half-life with dynamic exchange in the NPC, as our data is averaged over all populations in the cell (see Discussion).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Sec13.

claim: Some extremely long-lived proteins associated with the NPC in neurons were described by Savas et al. (2012) and Toyama et al. (2013) in an in-vivo study in rat brain.
source: Others have described some extremely long-lived proteins associated with the NPC in neurons (in-vivo study in rat brain; (Savas et al., 2012; Toyama et al., 2013); we also detect some of the same long-lived NPC components in our neural samples.
evidence: This describes findings from cited previous studies.
